title: Diary Entry Format: Layout, Rules and Examples
description: The diary entry format taught in schools: date, day and time, Dear Diary, body, closing and signature. Fill it in online, print it, and see marked examples.
h1: Diary entry format: layout, rules and examples
intro: The standard diary entry format has six parts: the **date**, the **day and time**, the salutation **Dear Diary**, the **body** written in the first person, a short **closing** thought, and your **signature**. Fill in the format below to practice, then print it or save it as a PDF.

fields.label: Opening line
fields.hint: One sentence about your mood or your day

fields.label: What happened
fields.hint: The main event, in order, in the past tense

fields.label: Closing thought
fields.hint: What you learned, hope or plan to do next

sections.h2: The diary entry format, part by part

blocks.p: This is the format most schools teach for diary writing. CBSE and many other school boards use this same basic layout in English writing tasks. Teachers and exam papers can differ on small points, such as where the time goes, so follow your own teacher's version if it is different.

head: Part
Position
Example
Tip
rows: Some formats put it on the same line
Use the name in the question

blocks.p: Here is how the parts sit on the page. Copy this shape into your notebook or exam paper.

example.label: Diary format
example.date:
Date: 14 March 2026
Day and time: Saturday, 9:30 pm
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
[Opening: one line about your mood or the day]
[Paragraph 1: what happened, in order]
[Paragraph 2: how you felt and why]
[Closing: a final thought, lesson or plan]
[Signature: your name]

blocks.tip: Some teachers ask you to write the date, day and time on three separate lines at the top left. Others accept them on one line. Both are common. Check which one your class uses.

sections.h2: What goes in the body of a diary entry

blocks.p: The body is where most of your marks come from. A strong body has three moves:

ol: **Set the scene.** Start with one sentence that shows your mood. "Today was the most nerve-wracking day of the term."
**Tell the event.** Who, what, where and when, in order, in the past tense. Pick the important details.
**Reflect.** How did it make you feel, and why? What did you learn? What will you do next?

head: Use
Tense
Example
rows: We reached the museum at ten.
I have never laughed so much.

blocks.p: **Question:** You are Riya. You visited an old age home with your school's social service club. Write a diary entry in about 120 words.

example.label: Sample answer
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
Today I learned more than I ever have in a classroom.
Our club visited the Sunrise old age home this morning.
We sang songs, served lunch and played carrom with the residents.
A lady named Mrs. Das told me stories about her school days.
She held my hand when we left and asked if we would come back.
I felt happy and a little sad at the same time.
They have so much love and so few visitors.
I have decided to visit once a month with my family.
Riya

ul: Date, day and time at the top.
Salutation **Dear Diary,** on its own line.
An opening line that sets the mood.
The event in order, in the past tense, with real details.
Clear feelings: happy, a little sad.
A closing decision and the signature from the question.

blocks.p: For more worked answers, see [how to write a diary entry](/how-to-write-a-diary-entry/) and our 14 [diary entry examples](/diary-entry-examples/).
Younger students use a simpler version of the same format. A date, Dear Diary, a few sentences about one thing that happened, how it felt, and their name.

example.label: Year 2 diary
example.title: Dear Diary,
example.text:
Today I went to the park with Grandma.
I went down the big slide by myself.
I felt brave and happy.
We had ice cream on the way home.
Love, Sam

blocks.p: There is a printable version made for young writers on our [diary template for kids](/diary-template-kids/) page, and more help on the [diary for kids](/diary-for-kids/) page.
Students often mix up diary writing and letter writing because both are personal. The format is different, and using letter parts in a diary entry can cost marks.

head: Diary entry
Informal letter
rows: News and questions for the reader
Yours lovingly, or similar, and your name
The person you send it to

blocks.p: Keep the diary entry private in tone. You are not telling someone else your news. You are thinking out loud about your own day. That is why feelings and reflection matter so much in this format.

blocks.h3: Diary format for a personal diary

blocks.p: Outside school, the format is much looser. Many people keep only the date and then write freely. Some use bullet points, some write a single line, and some never write Dear Diary at all. The school format is a good habit, though, because the date and a closing thought make old entries easier to understand later. For more on personal diaries, read [how to write a diary](/how-to-write-a-diary/).
Before you hand in your diary entry, check each point:

ul: Date, day and time are at the top left.
Dear Diary is on its own line with a comma.
Written in the first person (I, me, my).
Events are in the past tense.
There is a closing thought or plan.
The signature matches the name in the question.
It is close to the word limit.
No letter parts like an address or Yours sincerely.

faq.q: What is the correct format of a diary entry?
faq.a: The correct format has the date, day and time at the top left, followed by the salutation Dear Diary. Then comes the body, written in the first person, telling what happened and how you felt. End with a closing thought and your signature. This is the format taught in most schools.

faq.q: Where do you write the date in a diary entry?
faq.a: Write the date at the top left of the page, usually with the day and time on the same line or just below. Write the date in full, such as 14 March 2026, rather than using only numbers. Some teachers want the date, day and time on separate lines, so follow your class format.

faq.q: Is the time necessary in a diary entry?
faq.a: In many school formats, including the one commonly used for CBSE English, the date, day and time are all expected at the top. In a personal diary the time is optional. If you are writing for an exam, include it to be safe.

faq.q: What is the diary entry format for class 6?
faq.a: Class 6 uses the same basic format: date, day and time, Dear Diary, a body of about 100 to 120 words in the first person, a closing line and your name. The topics are usually everyday events like a school trip, a festival or a birthday.

faq.q: Should a diary entry have a title?
faq.a: Usually no. A school diary entry starts with the date and Dear Diary, not a title. In a personal diary you can add a title if you like it. Some teachers allow a short heading, so check their instructions. For exams, it is safest to leave it out.
